questions.prompt: In a cache-aside (lazy loading) strategy, what happens on a cache miss?

options.text: The request fails and is retried by the client
The write is queued until the cache is warm
The cache fetches from the database itself and returns the value
The application reads from the database and then populates the cache

questions.explanation: The application owns the logic: check cache, fall back to the database, then store the result. Only requested data is ever cached, at the cost of a slower first request per key.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of a write-through cache compared with write-back?

options.text: Writes are faster, but data can be lost on a crash
Reads are slower, but writes are safer
Writes are slower, but the cache and store never diverge
It removes the need for cache eviction

questions.explanation: Write-through commits to the backing store on every write, so nothing is lost but each write pays the store's latency. Write-back buffers in the cache and is faster, at the risk of losing unflushed data.

questions.prompt: What problem does a cache stampede (thundering herd) describe?

options.text: The cache returns data belonging to another user
Two caches hold contradictory values for one key
The cache runs out of memory and evicts everything
Many concurrent requests miss the same expired key and all hit the database

questions.explanation: A popular key expiring can send a burst of identical queries to the database at once. Mitigations include a lock so only one request recomputes the value, and adding jitter to expiry times.

questions.prompt: Why is consistent hashing preferred over simple modulo hashing for distributing keys across cache nodes?

options.text: It eliminates the need for cache expiry
It guarantees a perfectly even distribution of keys
Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys
It allows keys to be looked up without knowing the node count

questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing the node count remaps almost every key and empties the cache. Consistent hashing places nodes on a ring so only the keys owned by the changed node move.

questions.prompt: What does a TTL on a cache entry primarily provide?

options.text: A guarantee that the value is always current
A bound on how stale the cached value can become
Compression of the cached value
Protection against unauthorised reads

questions.explanation: A TTL trades freshness for simplicity: rather than tracking every change, you accept data can be out of date by at most that interval. Correctness-critical values need explicit invalidation instead.

questions.prompt: Which content is a CDN best suited to serve?

options.text: Static assets such as images, scripts and video segments
Write-heavy transactional database queries
Long-running background jobs
Per-user personalised account pages

questions.explanation: CDNs cache identical bytes at edge locations near users, cutting latency and origin load. Content that differs per user has no reuse, so caching it at the edge gains little.

questions.prompt: Why is the LRU eviction policy widely used in caches?

options.text: It guarantees the minimum possible number of misses
It exploits temporal locality; recently used items are likely to be used again
It requires no bookkeeping at all
It always evicts the largest item first

questions.explanation: LRU approximates the unimplementable optimal policy by assuming the recent past predicts the near future. It behaves badly on scans, which sweep the cache with data used exactly once.

questions.prompt: Cache invalidation is often called one of the hard problems in computing because:

options.text: Knowing exactly when cached data has become wrong is difficult across a distributed system
Caches cannot store structured data
Invalidation requires taking the system offline
Deleting a cache key is computationally expensive

questions.explanation: The write that invalidates a value may happen on another node, in another service, or in a batch job. Tracking every dependency is intricate, and getting it wrong serves stale data indefinitely.

questions.prompt: A read-heavy service adds a cache and the hit rate settles at 90 percent. What is the main effect on the database?

options.text: Write load falls by 90 percent
Read load falls to roughly one tenth of its previous level
Query latency at the database increases tenfold
The database can be removed entirely

questions.explanation: Only the 10 percent of reads that miss now reach the database. Writes still go through, and the database remains the source of truth that repopulates the cache.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of caching data at multiple layers (browser, CDN and application) simultaneously?

options.text: An update must be invalidated at every layer, or stale data persists at some of them
Total storage cost becomes unbounded
The database stops receiving writes
Requests are served twice

questions.explanation: Each layer expires independently, so purging the CDN does nothing for copies already in browsers. This is why versioned asset URLs are preferred: a new URL sidesteps invalidation entirely.
